title: Short Stuff: Turbulence
summary: A Short Stuff episode on airplane turbulence. The hosts open with a description of the three turbulence intensity levels (light, moderate, severe) and a reported Delta flight incident where a drink cart and flight attendant ended up on the ceiling. They discuss how rare turbulence injuries and deaths are, citing FAA figures (44 injuries in 2016 among more than nine million passengers, 13 in 2013, 17 in 2017, and three deaths between 1980 and 2008). They explain why planes are built to flex, the three main types of turbulence (convective, mountain wave, clear air), and how pilots avoid turbulence through flight planning, weather instruments, rerouting with air traffic control, and warnings from other pilots and ground networks. They close with advice to keep seatbelts fastened, a note that planes can create wake turbulence when following too closely, and a joke comparing it to tailgating.

segments.title: Opening banter and turbulence intensity levels
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on airplane turbulence, describe light, moderate, and severe categories, and recount a reported Delta flight where a drink cart and flight attendant ended up on the ceiling.

segments.title: Rarity of turbulence injuries and aircraft design
segments.summary: The hosts cite FAA injury figures and historical deaths, saying turbulence is rare. They explain that wings are designed to flex, comparing it to cars designed to crumple in crashes.

segments.title: Three types of turbulence
segments.summary: The hosts describe convective turbulence from thunderstorms, mountain wave turbulence from air cresting over mountains, and clear air turbulence at jet streams where air masses of different temperatures and speeds meet.

segments.title: How pilots avoid turbulence
segments.summary: The hosts explain that pilots plan routes in advance, use weather instruments to choose among storms, and request course changes or altitude changes from air traffic control.

segments.title: Mountain and clear air turbulence prediction and pilot communication
segments.summary: The hosts note mountains and lenticular clouds can help pilots predict turbulence, while clear air turbulence is hard to see. Pilots share information with each other and ground networks, giving warnings several minutes ahead, and passengers are told to sit down.

segments.title: Seatbelt advice, wake turbulence, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts advise keeping seatbelts fastened, warn that planes following too closely create wake turbulence, make a tailgating joke, and sign off.
